# The Last Watch of the Mara Celeste

I still make tea the same way. Loose leaf in a steel strainer, water just off the boil so it doesn't go bitter. I warm the mug first. I learned that from my mother, who cooked for the ferries out of Kaohsiung, and she learned it from her mother, who cooked for no one but did everything with that same attention, as though the object of your care had a right to the full weight of your competence regardless of whether it would notice. You warm the mug. You pour the water. You steep for three minutes if it's oolong, four if it's the cheap black, and you carry it with both hands because a thing made well deserves to arrive intact.

The night I'm thinking of, the second night of the typhoon, I boiled the water in a kettle I'd wedged between the stove rail and a rolled towel. The *Mara Celeste* was pitching maybe thirty degrees. Not the worst I'd seen on her—that would have been the crossing from Hualien two winters prior, when we lost the starboard davit and I served congee out of thermoses because nothing would stay in a bowl. But bad. The kettle slid against the towel and the towel held. I steeped the tea. Black, four minutes. I removed the strainer and set it in the sink where it could rattle all it wanted. Then I went up.

The ladder to the wheelhouse was seven rungs. I had climbed it thousands of times, in weather and out. You lead with your hip, keep the mug in your leeward hand, and you don't rush. I came up through the hatch and the wind hit different up there, a pressure in the ears more than a sound, and the rain on the windows was horizontal, constant, a white noise that after a while you stopped hearing the same way you stop hearing your own blood.

Captain Wen was at the wheel.

She was not fighting it. That was the first thing. I had seen her in heavy weather before—we all had, the whole of the years I'd been aboard—and she was a physical sailor, a woman who leaned into the wheel with her shoulders and cursed the sea in a dialect her grandfather had spoken, words I never learned but understood by their rhythm to be deeply profane and deeply affectionate, the way you swear at something you respect. But that night she stood still. Her hands were on the wheel at ten and two, her feet shoulder-width apart, her weight centered, and she was looking out the forward windows at nothing, because there was nothing to see. The sea and the sky had merged into a single moving darkness. She stood in it the way you stand in a doorway when you've decided not to go through.

I set the tea on the console beside the GPS unit. "Pressure's still dropping," I said, because I'd checked the barometer on my way up and because I didn't know what else to say.

"Mm," she said.

I stood there a moment. The console was cluttered—charts, a pencil, the handheld VHF, the log book with its cracked spine. Under the edge of the nav chart I could see the letters. I had seen them before. Everybody on the *Mara Celeste* had seen them, which was everybody, which was Wen and me. White envelopes, the bank's name in blue, the kind of blue they use when they want you to feel the institution behind the ink. The paper had gone soft in the damp. The edges curled upward like something trying to pull free. One of them had a figure circled in red—Wen's handwriting, her architect's numerals—and I looked at it long enough to see that the number was larger than anything the *Mara Celeste* could earn in two years of coastal freight, and then I looked away, because looking was already more than I had a right to.

"Get some sleep," I said.

"Soon," she said.

I went below. I checked the bilge pump, which was running but labored, a catch in its cycle like a cough that won't clear. I wiped the galley counter. I re-stowed two cans of condensed milk that had worked loose. Then I lay in my bunk and didn't sleep, because the ship was making sounds I knew and sounds I didn't, and the ones I didn't were lower, structural, the kind of sound a thing makes not when it's stressed but when it's considering whether to go on holding.

Maybe two hours later I went back up. I don't know why. I've asked myself so many times that the question has worn smooth, a stone I carry in my hand and can no longer read. I simply went up.

The tea was on the console where I'd left it. A skin had formed on its surface, pale and membranous, like the film on a cooling soup. The tea was stone cold. You could tell without touching it. Cold has a stillness that heat doesn't.

Wen hadn't moved. Not her hands, not her feet, not, as far as I could tell, her gaze. The storm was still there, unchanged, as though it had no interest in developing or resolving, and she was still there inside it, matching its indifference with her own.

I picked up the mug. She didn't turn. I went below and poured the tea into the sink and washed the mug and set it upside down on the drying rack, because that is what you do.

---

By morning the pumps had failed.

I don't mean they stopped—not at first. I mean the sound changed. The cough became a stutter, and then a kind of gargling aspiration, and then silence, and in the silence what came forward was the other sound, the one that had been there for hours underneath the mechanical rhythm: water moving inside the ship.

It is not like water in a bathtub or a pool. Those are contained. This was uncontained. It moved with the ship's roll but on its own schedule, a half-second behind, so that you felt the sea outside and then felt its echo inside, a call and response that meant the hull was no longer a distinction but a formality. The water hit the bulkheads with a sound like a palm slapping a table—flat, percussive, with a reverb that traveled through the steel and into your teeth. And between the slaps there was a groaning, long-voweled and phrasal, as though the ship were trying to form words in a language it was inventing as it died. I had heard steel groan before. This was not groaning. This was the sound of a thing discovering that it had limits.

Wen came into the galley at seven-fifteen. She sat in her usual seat, the one bolted to the deck by the porthole, and she said, "Deal."

We played every morning. Piquet, two-handed, a game her grandfather had taught her, which he'd learned from a French merchant sailor in a century that felt, aboard the *Mara Celeste*, only recently concluded. We played with a deck so used the cards were soft as cloth, their faces ghosted, the queen of hearts identifiable less by her printed image than by a coffee stain in her upper left corner that I knew better than I knew some people's faces.

I dealt. The water slapped the bulkhead on the other side of the galley wall, close enough to hear the air it displaced hissing through a seam in the steel. Neither of us mentioned it. Wen studied her hand. She discarded three and drew. I discarded two and drew. She opened with a point of five and I conceded it, and she took the trick with a king I should have seen coming because she always led kings when she had the point, every single time, a tell I had known for years and still fell for because there was a pleasure in falling for it, in being predictable inside a game whose outcome had never, between us, mattered.

"You miscounted," she said at one point.

"I didn't."

"Ten, jack, queen. That's three, not four."

"I had the nine underneath."

She looked. I showed her. She made a sound through her nose that was her version of conceding a point, and I marked it on the pad between us with the pencil stub we used, and the ship leaned and the water moved inside it with a sound like a body turning in a bed, and the pencil rolled off the pad, and I caught it before it hit the floor, and we kept playing.

I won by twelve points. She didn't congratulate me. She never did. She pushed back from the table and said, "I'm going up," and she went.

I gave it five minutes. I don't know why five. Then I followed.

She was on deck, in the rain, at the base of the mainmast. She had a length of line—eight-millimeter braided nylon, the kind we used for lashing cargo—and she was tying herself to the mast. Not quickly. Not frantically. With the same hands that had held the cards, the same measured attention. A bowline around her waist, snug but not tight, seated just above the hip bones. A figure-eight to the mast, wrapped twice for friction. Then a second bowline, redundant, because Wen was a woman who believed in redundancy, in the principle that anything worth securing was worth securing twice.

I stood in the hatchway. The rain was on my face. She didn't look at me. She tested the knots with a sharp pull—her full weight against the line, her boots sliding on the wet deck, her body tilting backward until the line caught and held—and then she stood upright and put her hand on the mast and looked out at the sea, which was not a sea any longer but a vertical world, walls of gray-green water erasing every distinction between up and down, and I could see, from where I stood, that the knots were perfect.

I went back to the galley. The cards were still on the table, fanned where we'd left them. The pad with our score was there, my handwriting, her point conceded. I gathered the cards. I squared the deck—tap the long edges, then the short edges, then the long edges again, the way she'd shown me. I put the deck in its box and put the box in the drawer and closed the drawer. I wiped the table. I put the pencil in the cup by the stove.

The water inside the hull had risen enough that I could hear it differently now—not slapping but lapping, almost gentle, as though it had won and could afford to be kind about it.

---

What I am going to tell you now I have told before, to the investigators in Keelung and to the woman from the maritime board and to a grief counselor the shipping company sent who sat across from me in a room that smelled like new carpet and asked me to describe my feelings, a request so alien to everything I had spent my life doing that I nearly laughed. I have told it to myself more times than any of them. I have told it in the dark in rented rooms and in the galley of the *Feng Hsing*, where I cooked for three years after, and in the backyard of my sister's house in Taitung, where I live now and where the only thing I am responsible for nourishing is a lime tree that does not require my competence but receives it anyway.

I was on deck. The *Mara Celeste* was low in the water, her bow already under, the stern rising in a way that made you understand that a ship does not sink—it is swallowed, taken in stages, the way the sea eats everything, patiently, from the edges.

Wen was at the mast. The line held her. Her hair was plastered to her face and her clothes were dark with water and she was looking at the horizon, which was not a line but an argument between the sea and the sky that the sea was winning.

She looked at me.

She smiled.

I need to be precise about this, and I cannot be, and that is the thing I carry. It was not a wide smile. It was not the smile of someone performing happiness for a witness. Her lips parted. The muscles around her eyes softened—released, the way a fist opens when sleep finally takes it. The rain was on her face. The smile reached her eyes and stayed there, and I saw in it something I had not seen since before the letters, before the calls from the bank, before the night she sat in the galley with the books spread out and did the arithmetic three times and put the pencil down and said nothing and I said nothing and we sat in a silence that I understood, then, was the sound of a future being foreclosed.

She smiled and it was the first time in months and I thought: *there you are*.

The horizon took her. It took the mast, and the deck, and then it rose to where I was and took me too, briefly—forty-seven minutes in the water, they tell me, though I remember none of it, only the cold and then the hull of the Panamanian freighter that pulled me out—and when I surfaced into the world that came after, I brought the smile with me.

I have turned it in my hands every day since. I have held it up to every light I know. It was relief—she was free of the bank and the debt and the slow dispossession of the only thing her grandfather had left her, the thing that was not a ship but a name, *Mara Celeste*, the beautiful and the heavenly, a name for a vessel that leaked and groaned and barely made its routes but carried in its steel the memory of a man who had built something with his hands and passed it to a woman who could not bear to let it be taken by strangers in suits. The smile was that. It was freedom from all of it.

But it was also something else, and this is where I fail.

It was directed at me. She looked at me and smiled, and in the smile was something I have spent years trying to name—gratitude, perhaps, or apology, or the particular tenderness of a person who knows she is about to cause an unsharable wound—and I cannot land on a single meaning because the smile was not single, it was not one thing, it was the whole of her, compressed into a facial expression that lasted maybe two seconds while the sea rose, and I was the only one there to receive it, and I received it, and I cannot tell you what I caught.

The deck of cards is in the drawer of the bedside table in my sister's guest room. I take them out some evenings. I lay out a hand of piquet and play both sides—mine and hers—and I make her mistakes for her, leading with kings when she has the point, because I don't want to win. I want the game to go on being the game it was. I want to sit across from someone in a galley that smells of oil and tea and hear the sea doing what the sea does and feel the ordinary friction of a life shared in a small space, where the stakes are twelve points and a pencil that rolls off the table.

I warm the mug. I steep the tea. I carry it to the table with both hands.

It goes cold. It always goes cold. But I make it right.
